memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Then Moses said to Aaron and his sons Eleazar and Ithamar, 'Do not let your hair become unkempt and do not tear your clothes, or you will die and the LORD will become angry with the whole community. But your relatives, all the Israelites, may mourn for those the LORD has destroyed by fire.'" - Lev 10:6 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
This is perhaps the hardest instruction in the chapter. Aaron may not mourn his own sons.

We must understand what is being asked and what is not. God is not forbidding grief itself — the rest of Israel is explicitly permitted to mourn. What is forbidden are the public rituals of mourning, performed by the acting high priest, in the middle of the tabernacle's inauguration.

Aaron was, at that moment, representing the entire nation before God. For the mediator to publicly break down over a judgement God had just declared righteous would have communicated something false to Israel about God's justice.

It was a specific instruction to specific men in a unique moment. It is not a rule that Christians should suppress grief. Jesus wept at Lazarus' tomb (Jn 11:35). Paul spoke of sorrow upon sorrow when a friend nearly died (Phil 2:27). We do not grieve like the rest of mankind, who have no hope (1 Thess 4:13) — but we do grieve.

Still, something real remains here. Sometimes obedience costs us the freedom to react as we would wish. Sometimes we must carry on with a duty while our heart is breaking.

God saw Aaron's silence. He always does.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Have I ever had to keep going in a responsibility while privately grieving?
2. Do I allow myself, and others, honest grief within a framework of hope?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, You see the grief I cannot always show. Give me strength to be faithful when my heart is heavy, and space to mourn honestly before You. Amen.
